content.title: THE FOOD SAFETY MISTAKES {{MOST KITCHENS}} MAKE WEEKLY
facts: **Chicken** – Washing it in the sink before cooking (splashes bacteria like Campylobacter onto your counters, not down the drain).
**Eggs** – Storing them in the fridge door (temperature swings every time it opens raise the risk of bacteria multiplying inside the shell).
**Melon** – Leaving cut pieces out on the counter for hours (the moist, sugary flesh is a prime breeding ground for Listeria and Salmonella).
**Ground beef** – Judging it's "done" by color alone (only a food thermometer hitting 160°F/71°C actually confirms harmful bacteria are killed).
**Garlic in oil** – Making your own and leaving it at room temperature (low-oxygen oil is exactly the environment Clostridium botulinum needs to grow).
**Leftover rice** – Cooling it slowly on the stovetop before fridging (Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and multiply fast as it cools).
**Frozen food** – Thawing it on the counter overnight (the outer layer sits in the bacteria "danger zone" for hours while the inside is still frozen).

caption:
A few of these are worth slowing down on. Chicken juice can splash further than you'd think when rinsed under a tap, landing on sponges, dish racks, and nearby produce that never gets cooked afterward — that's actually how a lot of kitchen cross-contamination starts. Ground beef is tricky because the pink-to-brown color change can happen before the inside ever reaches a temperature high enough to kill bacteria, which is why a thermometer beats "it looks cooked" every time. And homemade garlic-in-oil is deceptively risky: garlic is a low-acid food, and sitting in oil at room temperature creates a sealed, oxygen-poor pocket that's ideal for botulism-causing bacteria to grow, even though nothing looks or smells off. Everyone's kitchen habits are a little different, so it's worth double-checking your own routine against these.
